name: Ethylmorphine
addictionPotential: very addictive with a high potential for abuse
toxicity: potentially lethal when mixed with depressants like alcohol or benzodiazepines
summary: A medium-strength opioid analgesic and analogue of morphine. Considered less potent than morphine but more potent than codeine, and has been used in Germany for this reason. Said to have a 'ceiling' effect where no more euphoric effects occurs with increased dosing. The drug is under investigation for it's use as a maintainance drug in opioid dependence therapy.

pharmacology.text: The active metabolites of ethylmorphine, notably morphine, exert their effects by binding to and activating the μ-opioid receptor. This occurs because opioids structurally mimic endogenous endorphins which are naturally found within the body and also work upon the μ-opioid receptor set. The way in which opioids structurally mimic these natural endorphins results in their euphoria, pain relief and anxiolytic effects.

uses.text: Ethylmorphine, also known as codethyline and dionine, is a semi-synthetic morphinan opioid first created by Merck in 1884 and used as a weaker alternative to morphine. Today, it is most commonly used as an antitussive which is available in cough syrup preparations like Cocillana, Cosylan, Solvipect comp. Ethylmorphine is also used in ophthalmic preparations as dionine to treat inflammations of the eye.
uses.brands: Cosylan, Diolan, Dionina, Diosan, Solvipect, Trachyl

sideEffects.text: Adverse effects are similar to other opioids and include drowsiness, constipation, vertigo, nausea, vomiting, and respiratory depression. Contraindications include asthma, respiratory insufficiency, and age under eight. Ethylmorphine may affect the user's ability to drive and operate heavy machinery, and may cause chemical dependence or addiction at high doses.
